utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The proceedings will continue in closed session for the next part of our proceedings regarding Mr. Milan Simic. The Trial Chamber has looked at the joint requests by the Prosecution and the Defence of Mr. Milan Simic for a closed session of the proceedings to follow according to Rule 62 ter (C). The Trial Chamber is of the view that there was no basis for the submission made by the Prosecution for a closed session for these proceedings. Paragraph 5 of the submission was simply stated without more. So the Trial Chamber is not satisfied that proceedings should be held in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe the Prosecution can make some further submissions on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honours please, essentially the -- the essence of the application is contained in paragraph 5, and I can understand why the Chamber is troubled by the lack of detail in that particular paragraph. Since or, rather, I should say prior to lunch, I contacted the officer in charge of the case, the investigating officer in this particular case who happens to be in Bosnia currently taking 92 bis statements. I had a fairly unsatisfactory telephone conversation with him, unsatisfactory because the telephone line was not very good and unsatisfactory also because it was secure and I had to use and he had to use guarded language. But essentially I went over the history of this case with him and his concerns because it was his concerns that originally caused this application to be made, and they are essentially this: When another defendant in this case, Mr. Todorovic, pleaded guilty and the plea agreement between the Office of the Prosecutor and that defendant became known, a number of witnesses in this case, witnesses who are to give evidence in this case, have given evidence in this case, expressed their considerable displeasure at that plea agreement, the fact of the plea agreement, and commented that they considered their continuing to provide evidence to the Tribunal in support of this particular Prosecution was a worthless exercise or something that they shouldn't continue to do any longer. It was no insignificant matter. I'm told that the particular officer and the Prosecutor who was formerly in charge of this case, Ms. Nancy Paterson, in fact had to travel to Bosnia on a ten-day mission to placate witnesses, explain as best they could various reasons why that particular plea agreement had been entered into between the Office of the Prosecutor and essentially get the witnesses back on board, and they were able to do so after providing an explanation. The officer who has been dealing with these witnesses for some years now has expressed to me very serious -- his serious concerns that if this particular plea agreement becomes known, it will have an adverse effect upon the willingness of the witnesses to continue to come here and give evidence in this case. So that essentially is the reason why this particular motion has been made. I can -- there are a few other matters that I want to also address the Chamber on and are related to this. First of all, I think it's important to point out and I understand the Chamber knows, but I wish to emphasise, of course, we're not seeking any sort of permanent suppression order or permanent non-disclosure of the plea agreement, the fact of the plea and of course the sentence which under Rule 100, I believe it is, has to be made public. It's only a temporary measure and I emphasise that it's only a temporary measure and the measure is only being sought until the closure of the Prosecution case so that the public nature, the desire to make public plea agreements will eventually be satisfied that the point of the Rule will essentially be satisfied. It's a question of when in the Prosecution's submission, and no deleterious consequences will flow if it's made known at a later point, namely at the close of the Prosecution case. The Defence support the Prosecution in this particular motion. You can see that it's a joint motion. That's the highest that I can put the matter at at the moment. If, however, the Chamber is not satisfied with that, then I would request that you provide suppression of the details of the publication -- of the plea agreement until such time as I can contact my officer and get his evidence, his account of things into proper form and perhaps provide you with more detail of the consequences for the -- that we fear may come about if the plea agreement is made public at this particular stage. In other words, I can marshal whatever evidence I can get from the officer in charge of the case and put it before you in a more orderly fashion if you're not satisfied with what I've told you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Any submission on the part of Mr. Milan Simic? Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for giving us this opportunity of this hearing because we've been working on this for a long time. Actually, the Defence does not have any problem with this hearing being public. However, in a spirit of cooperation, when we were negotiating this plea agreement, we do understand the reasons why our learned colleagues from the Prosecutor's side are requesting the closed session, and that is why we joined them in our joint motion for the closed session. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will adjourn to consider the submissions of the Prosecution for 20 minutes. --- Break taken at 2.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has considered the submissions made by the Prosecution on their -- on the parties' joint request for these proceedings to be held in closed session, and the Trial Chamber is satisfied that good cause has been shown for the proceedings to be held in closed session according to Rule 62 ter (C), in particular that in these proceedings, this is the second time that an accused has entered into a plea agreement and that the impact upon the rest of the Prosecution witnesses will be even far greater when -- if the proceedings are held in open session, most likely the Prosecution may have greater difficulty in persuading the rest of the witnesses to continue giving evidence in these proceedings. So the proceedings will go ahead in closed session. The Chamber has before it a joint motion for consideration of a plea agreement between the accused Milan Simic and the Office of the Prosecutor. The motion was filed jointly by counsel for Mr. Milan Simic and the Prosecution on a confidential basis on 13th May 2002. According to the plea agreement attached to the joint motion, the accused Milan Simic agrees to plead guilty to counts 4 and 7, which are two counts of torture charged as crimes against humanity of the amended indictment, while the Prosecutor has agreed to move for leave to withdraw the remaining charges against the accused Milan Simic if the guilty plea -- the guilty plea to the two counts is accepted by the Trial Chamber. The plea agreement contains provisions reflecting the understanding of the accused Milan Simic as to the nature of count 4 and count 7, including the legal elements of torture as a crime against humanity, and the factual basis agreed upon as a basis for his guilty plea to the two counts. The plea agreement also recommends a range of sentences based on the understanding that such recommendation is not binding on the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber has observed that the plea agreement has also been filed in the B/C/S language which the accused Milan Simic understands and is attached to the joint motion. The Trial Chamber has looked at the provisions of the relevant Rules, in particular Rule 62 ter, and we'll deal with the proceedings under Rule 62 bis and would like to address the accused Mr. Milan Simic at this stage. Mr. Simic, the Trial Chamber would like to find out from you whether you understand the details of this plea agreement you entered into with the Prosecution. THE ACCUSED M. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I did understand them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber would also like to find out from you whether when entering into this plea agreement you understand that the Trial Chamber is not bound to accept the range of sentences agreed to by yourself and the Prosecutor. THE ACCUSED M. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber would also like to ask you whether you fully discussed with your counsel the plea agreement, and he advised you of the consequences of pleading guilty to the two charges. That's count 4 and count 7. THE ACCUSED M. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I have discussed it with my counsel, and he advised me of all possible consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber would like to know whether you were threatened or coerced in any way to make this agreement. THE ACCUSED M. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No, I was not coerced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It was entirely made by you voluntarily? THE ACCUSED M. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber would like to put the counts to you so that you can plead as advised and according to your own free will, and that is count 4 of the charges as detailed in the plea agreement. How do you plead to count 4 of the amended indictment charging you with torture? THE ACCUSED M. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I plead guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber again asks you to plead to count 7 of the amended indictment charging you with torture. How do you plead? THE ACCUSED M. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I plead guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Trial Chamber records pleas of guilty for both counts, on count 4 and count 7. The Trial Chamber has considered the particulars of the facts in the plea agreement and is satisfied that they do form sufficient factual basis for finding the accused guilty on both counts and makes a finding of guilty and enters the conviction for both count 4 and count 7 against the accused Milan Simic accordingly. The Trial Chamber would like to ask the Prosecutor, because according to the plea agreement, it is indicated that the Prosecution intends to apply for leave to withdraw the remainder of the charges against the accused Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honours please, Mr. Milan Simic, having entered pleas of guilty to counts 4 and 7, and the Trial Chamber having accepted those pleas of guilty to those two counts, 4 and 7, the Prosecution seeks the leave of the Trial Chamber to withdraw the remaining counts laid against Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Trial Chamber grants leave for the Prosecution to withdraw the remaining counts against Mr. Milan Simic, and the Trial Chamber orders that the Prosecutor should file confirmation of withdrawal in writing by next week Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will move to the next stage, about the possible date for hearing on sentencing and would like to find out from both parties how they intend to make their submissions on sentencing. Of course the Trial Chamber would appreciate submitting any evidence, if any has to be called by the parties in the form of statements, to avoid taking too much time. So the Prosecution, can you indicate how much time you think you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I find that a little difficult at this stage to say with any precision because I haven't prepared any submissions, of course. The Prosecution would seek to provide the Chamber with both a written submission and accompanied by some oral submissions. I have discussed the timing of those submissions with my colleagues, counsel for Mr. Milan Simic, and we agreed that early July would be -- of course if that's suitable to the Chamber, would be an appropriate time to deliver those submissions. As to the time required for the Prosecution to present its submissions -- may I just have a brief moment to confer with may colleague Mr. Weiner, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Than you. Thank you for that opportunity to speak to my colleague. At this stage, the Prosecution is not minded to attempt to call any evidence on the plea, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On the sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On the sentencing issue, sorry. And we expect at this stage to confine ourselves to legal submissions on sentencing law and how it applies to this particular case. And with the benefit of some written submissions, I would hope that we would be able to complete all of our submissions within about one and a half to two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Defence of Mr. Milan Simic? Mr. -- Ms. Baen?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We too plan on filing written submissions or a brief, and we have discussed it, and we think we have a total of about eight witnesses that we'd like to call, and we're going to try to do the majority of those in the form of an affidavit or stipulations of evidence we're working on with the Prosecution right now so that we can make the hearing as short as possible. But it's going to depend on whether or not we can get affidavits from these people or whatever we decide is best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Usually if it's -- normally to be evidence regarding character.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's character and mitigation and also maybe psychiatrists probably in the form of a report. I don't know whether that would be live or not. Possibly the doctor who's been treating Mr. Simic here, but nothing out of the ordinary. Just mitigation, character witnesses, and doctors. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because the Trial Chamber is interested in economising on time that the proceedings will take. Very well. The Trial Chamber will issue a Scheduling Order on the matters for further hearing in these proceedings. This is the end -- yes, Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: This may be my last chance to address the Chamber for a while, so it is somewhat difficult because I live in the United States and Mr. Zecevic lives in Serbia, and so we sort of propose a schedule on all the work that we would have to do to get our brief done and get our witnesses together, and we came up with a date of the -- I think as Mr. Di Fazio said, of the end of June we would prefer to file our brief then if it's appropriate with the Trial Chamber and then possibly argue sentencing the week after that. We've discussed this somewhat at length, and consideration also that the Prosecutors will continue in the trial daily. We felt this might be most appropriate for both parties, but of course it's up to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But I just want it to be clear. You would prefer the hearing to be in the first week of July then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: We would prefer the first week of July, and we would prefer to file our briefs the end of June and then argue the next week and then probably take not more than one day of the Court's time for the sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I just support what Ms. Bane says and can I emphasise, if I may, the end of June, for the very end of June, if I can emphasise that, for the written submission. And again, I have no problem with early July. The reason I say that is it's going to be the beginning of June and the middle of June is going to be, I think, a particularly busy time for the Prosecution for various reasons, and we would like to be able to -- we'll need some time to concentrate on this and research the matter and get our submissions into good and useful form for you. So may I urge upon you the provision of the written submission at the very end of June if that's suitable, of course, to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well -- yes. Very well. The Trial Chamber will consider that when making the Scheduling Order. This is the end of the matter on the plea, and the Trial Chamber considers that we can proceed with the rest of the proceedings right away, except that the next witness will be in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we can go ahead and -- Ms. Baen, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this time is the Trial Chamber going to -- are you going to wait to sever us until you get the written submissions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, confirmation by the -- the withdrawal in writing by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then the Trial Chamber will go ahead and probably separate the trials for the better continuation of the proceedings and also to avoid unfairness on the rest of the accused persons proceeding on the indictment that the Prosecutor will choose to continue with. Can we have the blinds opened, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that we shall take the normal time, go on with the proceedings for one and a half hours before the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm confused. Do you mean we're going to take a break in five minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- for the normal period or we'll take an hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, one and a half hours because we took a break just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Will the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the could the your name, please?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: My name is Hajrija Drljacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st of April, 1932.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: So you're 70 years old now?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Divorced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I have one daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Any grandchildren?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Three. And one great grandchild.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was born in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you live most of your life?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was just born in Brcko. I lived my whole life in Bosanski Samac, except for the wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did your parents live their lives?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: My father was born in Bosanski Samac and spent his whole life there, as did my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when did you father's family first come to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: My great grandfathers settled there in the 1880s. They were the first settlers, among the first settlers in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have any brothers or sister?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: We were eight children, three sisters and five brothers. One sister and one brother died, and we remain six.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And of those six, how many lived in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: All except for one brother who lived in brother [As interpreted], and one sister lived in Serbia. The rest of us lived in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now your brother who died prior to the war, where did his wife and children live?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Safet's wife and children lived in Bosanski Samac since they were born. In fact, his wife was originally from Orasje, and they lived -- she lived with the children in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, your sister who passed away, when did she -- when did she die?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I found her deceased on the 12th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did she die from?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: She died of hunger, cold, and fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was she living when she passed away?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me [Interpretation] From the day she was born until the day she died, she lived in Bosanski Samac, and she was ill for a while before she died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated -- you indicated you lived in Bosanski Samac your whole life. Where did you -- where did you live?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I lived in Bosanski Samac with the exception of seven years, when I lived in Osijek, where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me just step back for one second. All these brothers and sisters who lived in Samac, are they still living there now?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Of my brothers and sisters, nobody is left in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why aren't they still in Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: One brother lived in Zagreb even before the war for about ten years. One brother and one sister died, and the rest of us had to leave Samac. We were forced to leave Samac because of the events there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated you lived in Samac. Where did you live in that town?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I lived in Pero Bozic Street, number 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that an apartment, house, or was that a -- was that a separate home?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: It was an apartment building. I lived in one apartment in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you work in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Except for these seven years, I had spent all my remaining work-life in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you work?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The last 20 years, I worked for Tekstilac. Afterwards, we were integrated with Mladost, and then the company changed its name into Sit, the Samac textile industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you do for Tekstilac and Mladost?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was an accountant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In April of 1992, were you still working or had you retired?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I retired at the end of 1998. Actually, I apologise. I was retired at the end of 1987, early 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what religion or ethnic group do you consider yourself to be a member of?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: My religion is Muslim, and I am a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever own any guns?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I have never owned any.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Ever a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Never, not even during the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Having lived your whole life in Bosanski Samac, I'm going to ask you about a few people. Do you know a man by the name of Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And knowing him very well, could you look around the courtroom and tell me if he's in this courtroom at this time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: He's the first one on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what colour is his shirt?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you look around and tell me if he's in this courtroom at this time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is, in the middle. Over there in the middle. The one with the moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you know a man by the name of Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I know Blagoje Simic only by sight. I have never had any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And does anyone look familiar in this courtroom like the Blagoje Simic you know by sight?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Maybe. I'm not sure. Maybe this gentleman that is writing right now could be him, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic lived with my sister. They lived in the same hallway. But people change. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that the defendant Simo Zaric and Miroslav Tadic were identified, and she indicated that Blagoje Simic may be the individual that she remembered, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let us move to January 1992 to mid-April of that same year. Where were you during that time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was in Croatia, because my daughter lived there. This was the time of the war in Croatia, and I travelled with her. She was a refugee with three little children. I returned on the 15th of April, 1992, to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were you home on April 17, 1992, at about 3.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th, after 6.00, and also on Thursday and on Friday I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move --

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: To my misfortune.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move to April 17th of that year, about 3.00 a.m., 3.00 in the morning. Did something happen in those early morning hours?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly what time it was, but you could hear loud shots. I didn't know what was going on. I hadn't been to Samac. I hadn't been there the previous two or three months, and I didn't know what was going on. For me, this was a great surprise, because I never expected anything similar to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you go outside or did you look out the window?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Only when I heard explosions in the vicinity. This explosion happened at the pizzeria, and I saw it from my window. I saw smoke. This explosion happened before that, and I saw smoke, and then I looked through the window. I was on the third floor. And I saw soldiers. These soldiers had the same uniforms as I saw in Croatia. They were camouflage uniforms. I thought it was the Croatian army that arrived. And I tried to get advice from my neighbours. I went to the first neighbour, the second neighbours, but they weren't home. I didn't know what to do. I was completely alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sometime later that morning, around 9.00 or 10.00, did you go to visit any of your other neighbours downstairs?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Kikarujof [phoen] lived downstairs. All of Samac knew him as Cika Juro even though he is not my relative. We called him that way because he was an older man. That would mean uncle Juro". I rang his doorbell, and people who were in his apartment came out. They were all surprised that I came back, and they said that I came from Osijek the day before the previous day. And she asked me, "Where were you last night?" And I said, "I was in my apartment." And when they asked me who I was with, I said I was alone. And then they told me I should have come to stay with them and I said, "Well, I didn't expect anything." I had no idea what was going on and I didn't know what could happen. We were discussing like this -- we were discussing my arrival, and at that moment, the front door was burst open, the front door of our entrance, and people downstairs asked who was there, and Dragica, uncle Juro's wife said, "There is nobody here." And I said, "We're all here." While we were talking like this, five soldiers came up to us and they had their rifles pointing at us, and they asked us, "What are you doing?" We were very confused. I don't quite remember what we said. But then they said that everybody should go their own apartment and they should also show -- we should all show them our IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take it a little slowly. Five soldiers came into the hallway of the apartment building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated they were armed. How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They were armed. They had camouflage uniforms on. They had black knitted caps, and they had marks, coloured marks on their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you know any of these five soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did two of them come from?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: One of them grew up in Samac. Whether he was born there or not, I don't know. His mother's name was Ruza the Italian, Ruza Italijanka [phoen]. That's how they called her. I know they called him Cera, something like that, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the other?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The other one was the brother of my former neighbour. I had known him as a child. He would come stay with his sister. He was of Orthodox religion. He was from Croatia. He was not Bosnian. But I knew him through his sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was -- and do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: His last name was Vukovic. I don't remember his first name. But amongst ourselves, we gave him the nickname Majmun, the monkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you knew two of these five people, two of these five soldiers. What about the other three? Did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was sure that the other three men came from Serbia, because they spoke in the Ekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And having lived so long in Bosanski Samac, did you recognise them as locals?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, Cera grew up in Samac. Whether he was born there or are moved later, I don't know. I know him more through his mother because she worked at the same company where I used to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the other three that you thought were -- that had these Serbian accents. Did you recognise them as being locals from Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at that time or at some later time, the next day, did you see any patches that those three people with the Serbian accents that you thought came from Serbia had on them, on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was very confused. I didn't notice anything at the time. I didn't really look. I didn't know where to look. But I did see at my neighbour's that her door was down, and it had some kind of a patch on his arm, this person that broke down her door, and it had a grey wolf on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated these five soldiers, the two locals and the five -- I'm sorry, the two locals and the three from Serbia ordered you to go to your apartments. What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Everybody went to their apartment. I wasn't gathered enough to find my ID. The previous Thursday I had been to the doctor, and I had a health card, and that's what I took with me. But this Vukovic man, he knew me so he didn't really take a look into my ID. He entered my apartment and asked me if I had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did you respond to soldier Vukovic when he asked you if you had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: "I do not." I said to him that I didn't. He went into my apartment. He was lifting cushions from the sofa. He was opening wardrobes. He looked through everything and then he left the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What were the other soldiers doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: At that time, you could hear loud noises, and I didn't know what was going on. After things got quieter, I saw that seven tenants weren't there and their apartments were broken into. That's what the soldiers did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was breaking into those other apartments?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Those five soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what happens next?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: After this man called Cera went to the fourth floor, I was on the hall on the third floor. He asked for the key so he could go up to the roof where he claimed a sniper was, but Cika Juro said that nobody had a key, that Babic Milan had the key.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was Babic Milan.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he was. Seven tenants weren't there. They were gone. Of these seven tenants, six were Serbs and one of them had a mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did Cera do after he was unable to get onto the roof because there was no key?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: He said, "Hello, black eagle here," through his walkie-talkie, and he told him he couldn't find the key.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he -- did he say the name of the person he was speaking with? Do you recall the name?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said Crni, which means black.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he told Crni that his code name was black eagle -- I'm sorry, was eagle?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell Crni on that radio, over that radio? What did he tell Crni?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: He told him about the key, that he couldn't find the key, so he couldn't go up to the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he stay very long after that?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Only as long as it took them to search the apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Cera have any conversation with you before he left your apartment building?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He ordered me that I had to keep an eye on the two apartments that were on my floor so that nobody could take anything out of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And people of what ethnic group resided in those apartments?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: As I said, there was six Serbs and one was a mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But two apartments on your floor, of what ethnic group with those persons?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs. Names Milan Babic and last name Maslic. I can't remember the first name right at this moment. If you will excuse me for a second. Velimir Maslic. The second tenant was called Maslic Velimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, after they left the apartment, did anything else happen on that date?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I went to my apartment, and I was inside. I didn't pay any attention, and I only asked the next day whether I could go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on the next day or the day after, the second or third day after the war started, did you notice anything on your front door, the front door to the building?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It said that we, that is to say Muslims and Croats, had to wear white armbands and that they could move freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So this was some sort of notice posted on the door?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Everybody said that -- people amongst themselves talked that we shouldn't leave the house without a white armband.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, on the door was a notice of some kind, a notice or a letter?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did you feel about that, having to wear an armband?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Of course we older people had learnt from the past. I immediately remembered the Second World War, when while I watched my fellow townspeople wearing white -- yellow bands. I was talking about the Jews that one morning just disappeared. Nobody had been left. And I expected us to have that same fate, all of us that had to wear the armbands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you discuss the armbands, the wearing of armbands with your neighbours and colleagues?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: We Muslims were allowed to talk amongst ourselves, but we had no right to ask anyone of the Orthodox people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there a discussion as to who issued that order, that notice that was on your door?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: We talked amongst ourselves, and I found out that it was done by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During those first three days after the war began, did people go somewhere to get their food, their milk and bread?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. We got certain items free in front of the local commune. We all got these items free, all of us, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was distributing those items?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross was distributing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you went to the local commune to get those food items, were you wearing your white armband?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Naturally. We weren't allowed to go out without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else wearing the white armbands?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats wore them. There is a videotape about this made by Cvijan Marinkovic. He taped us while we were waiting in the line to get milk and bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was this videotape ever shown anywhere?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: We saw similar tapes. I didn't see myself, but we saw them through Belgrade while we had electricity. Afterwards we didn't have electricity, so we couldn't watch anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you went out, did you see any soldiers on the streets?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing white armbands?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: No. They had something on their shoulder with three colours, these three colours. I don't know what they signified. Somebody had just one of them, somebody had two, somebody had three colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you pointed --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: For the record, she pointed toward the top of her shoulder towards her neck, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If you like, I could have her demonstrate again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Was it the left shoulder or the right shoulder?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was it the left shoulder or the right shoulder or both?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Whether it was the left or right or both, I can't be sure, but I know they were there. Whether the left or the right, but do I know they have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it's on one of the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At the top of the shoulder, close to the neck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how long did the Red Cross supply bread and milk?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: First days of the war. Later we could buy them at the grocery store or in the market, whatever there was to be bought. At the beginning, there was only one store that was working, that was selling bread, and we could go there and buy bread if we were -- if it was available on at that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Before that, I just want to ask you, do you know a man by the name of Omer Nalic?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see him during the first three or four days of the war?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And tell the Court the situation where you saw Omer Nalic.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They beat Omer Nalic very much. They showed him -- they took him around town all bloodied, and they were putting him on display so that the rest of us would be scared and leave Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," who was taking him around town on a truck all bloodied?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, the people that were fighting. Those that allegedly liberated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are you referring to the soldiers from the Republika Srpska and the 4th detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Republika Srpska didn't exist at the time. It might have been the people from the 4th Detachment. And they said that they liberated us, and I was wondering who from. They liberated us from freedom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you would go to a grocery store, that there was one grocery store that was open. Where was that grocery store located?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: It was at the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how often did you go to that grocery store?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you wearing your white armband when you went there almost every day?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Of course. Without fail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were any Serb civilians wearing white armbands?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Never. It was us who were marked for destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you went to these -- when you went to this store wearing your armband, were you always able to buy food at the local grocery store?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: It all depended on the shop assistants. Sometimes they would give it to us, sometimes not. If they wouldn't, we could do nothing about it even if we could very well see that there was bread available. And it only happened to us Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why wouldn't they sell you bread or milk?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They were just venting their base instincts, taking advantage of us. We had no right to complain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did they say -- what did they say to you when they wouldn't let you buy food?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They would say, "No bread." We could see it very well on the -- on the shelves. I could see it, but I wouldn't argue. I would just leave the shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Serb civilians that were refused to be sold any bread?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any other shops in Bosanski Samac where you could buy food?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The only shop selling bread was the one I mentioned. I'm talking about bread now. At the marketplace, we could buy what was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So if they would not sell you -- if they would not sell the bread to the Muslims and Croats at that grocery store, you could not get bread?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there any butcher shops that were open where you could get meat?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was one private shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they sell you meat?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's continue. At that early stage during the spring of 1992, would you be mainly at home or outside during that time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I would mainly stay at home and go out only when I had to. I sort of avoided going out because of this armband I had to wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever listen to the radio while you were home during the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I did. I listened to the radio. It was particularly painful to listen to one broadcast when Simo Zaric was speaking. He was telling the most awful things about us Muslims, that we should disappear, that we have no roots, no origin, that we were nobodies. Here he is sitting right there, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take it slow. You were listening to the radio. While you were listening to the radio, you heard the defendant Zaric speaking?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I listened to him, and I can confirm this while looking him straight in the eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how did you know it was Simo Zaric? Did they announce -- did he introduce himself? Did they announce his name? How do you know it was Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, his voice is no less recognisable than my own. Samac is a small town with a population of less than 10.000. We all know one another. I know where everybody's from, everybody's roots.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they ever announce his name on the radio show or on the radio programme?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That wasn't really necessary. Maybe they did; maybe they didn't. It was widely known that it was Zaric speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you recognised his voice and recognised Simo Zaric on that radio station?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yes, of course. It wasn't just that one broadcast. Perhaps it was a tape that was repeated several times a day for several days for a long, long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were derogatory statements about Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about extremists?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Of course. All Muslims are extremists, and everybody was saying that there were some lists of names. Muslims were named who were supposedly intending to destroy Serbs in Bosanski Samac. But we never saw that list. They always threatened with this list and used it as a pretext when taking people allegedly to be interviewed or questioned. They mentioned this list as including people who intended to do some sort of evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, apparently the technicians need to pause to change the tapes. They need approximately a one-minute pause. I could do so right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can just wait for them to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, before you continue, I wonder whether you could seek a clarification. Page 40, line 19. When the witness says in answer your -- your question was: "Was there any discussion about extremists on the radio?" And the answer was: "Of course. All Muslims are extremists," et cetera, et cetera. Could the witness tell us whether that was what she heard on the radio, because otherwise it's a bit oblique the way it sounds there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I had several questions along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: First I want to apologise, ma'am, for the interruption. The technicians had to change a tape in the system. So we'll continue on. I have some questions to clarify a few statements. All right. Now, I asked you if there was any discussion on that radio show involving Simo Zaric about extremists -- or actually, on the radio show was there any discussion about extremists, and you said, "Of course. All Muslims are extremists." Did someone on that radio show make that statement?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Right. They did. "Muslim extremists." It's a direct quote. "Muslim extremists." Sometimes they would say Muslim and Croat extremists. Oftentimes they called us Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: People. People of Orthodox Christian faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But who on the radio show? Who was making those statements about the Muslims or the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric say anything about the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They were the heavenly people, the heavenly nation. That's what they called themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did Simo Zaric make that reference to the Serb as being a heavenly nation?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: All of them. All of them were calling themselves the nation, in fact, the heavenly nation. Everybody, including Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was he calling, referring to the Serbs a heavenly nation at the same time that he was saying derogatory remarks about the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, specifically on that radio programme, whether he mentioned the heavenly nation, maybe, yes, maybe not. I don't know. But he was saying that Muslim and Croat extremists were going to destroy the Serb people. That's what he said. And when referring to them, to themselves, he would say that Serbs were a heavenly, celestial nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did Simo Zaric ever use the word Ustasha when he spoke on the radio?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They were saying that Ustashas were going to come before them, and they had come first instead as liberators. Ustashas were mentioned so often that I don't really remember the specific situations any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. You keep on saying "they." Was Simo Zaric using those phrases, using that term when he was speaking on the radio, "Ustasha"?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that this word was repeated so often that I don't even remember any more the specific occasions. But yes, he did. He was prone to -- to say "Ustashas." I would hear him in the street. I didn't listen to the radio that much, but other people would tell me later about programmes that I personally didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mention that also on the radio there was discussion of lists, of some lists being found. Could you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, they were saying -- Serbs were saying that they were in possession of lists from which you could see the names and surnames of Muslims as well as Serb members whose houses were going to be burnt or families killed, and they used this as a pretext when taking people to interrogations from which they never came back before they were exchanged. However, we never saw those lists, as a matter of fact. And if they exist at all, I would appreciate it if the gentleman would show them to me so I could see who was going to kill whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on. Let's move on with just one question. With regard to the lists that were mentioned on the radio station, did Simo Zaric, did the defendant Simo Zaric, ever mention those lists or describe or discuss those lists on the radio show?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, specifically on the radio, I don't know. I didn't listen to everything. However, all of them, all Serbs told us and told me specifically that there were lists naming names of Muslim extremists who were going to destroy -- whether it was one man or one family or one house, I don't know. In any case, those lists were in the Serbs' possession. And I'm saying again, if those lists exist, I would like to see them. And let these gentlemen show the Trial Chamber these lists to prove who was going to do what.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- let's move on into May -- early to mid-May of 1992. Do you recall another notice being placed on your front door, the front door to your building?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let me try and refresh your recollection. Do you recall any notices being placed in relation to gathering of persons?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's right. Sorry. I couldn't remember it straight away. There was a notice on my entrance door and all around town banning the gathering of more than two Muslims or Croats. Up to two were allowed to assemble.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said it was on your front door and all around town. Where were these notices posted around town?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Everywhere. On shop windows, on walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, also about that time - we're talking about early to mid-May - did something happen to the telephones belonging to the Muslims and Croats of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: One day they disconnected the telephones of all Muslims and Croats. We no longer had any lines connecting us to the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have a telephone?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was it working up until that point?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: No. Well, up until that point, you mean. Up until that point, it was working. At first I thought there was something wrong with my telephone. I tried to put a call through and couldn't. I couldn't get the dial tone. And later, I learnt that they disconnected everybody's telephones at the same time. I learned that from my brothers and from my fellow townsfolk, but only Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about your Serb neighbours? Did they have telephones and were they working?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They did have telephones, and we heard them ringing. I personally heard them ringing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, up until that point while you were phone was still functioning, would you ever contact any of your relatives outside of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I contacted my brother in Zagreb, my sister in Negotin, and my daughter in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your sister in Negotin, where is that located, Negotin?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Negotin is in Republika Srpska. No. No. In Serbia. In the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after your phone was disconnected, could you speak with your sister in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: My sister who was living in the Republic of Serbia, I had no contact with her until October 1993, when I first managed to make a call.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. The telephones were disconnected in May of 1992. You first spoke with your sister in October of 1992 or October of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And please tell the Court how did you go about contacting your sister?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: She had a work colleague who was also a close friend, and this woman told me that I could use her phone. She told me to come to her home and that my sister would call me on Wednesday at 12.00. And we continued this practice. Every Wednesday at noon, I would talk to my sister from the house of this colleague and friend of my sister's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And this colleague or friend of your sister's, where did she live? In what town?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: She lived in Bosanski Samac. They had been to school together, and they worked to the until the time when my sister left for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how come her telephone was functioning and yours wasn't?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: She was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did something happen in November with this friend of your sister?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: She apologised and said that she couldn't allow me to talk from her home any more. And I learned at that time that the public phone at the post office was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you go to the post office and use that public telephone?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I went to the post office every day at 12.00 because my sister's husband was very ill, and every day at 12.00 I went there to call and to see how they were, how they had spent the night, how they had eaten, slept. Every day at noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the post office every day, did anyone bother you as you walked to and from the post office?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: All kinds of things happened. Among other things, I'll tell you about the time when a group of teenagers chanted after me, "I don't like you, Alija, because you are a balija." The time came for Serbs to take their revenge and for the mosques to be blown up." And they would finish this with a ululating type of sound typical of Serbian folk songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when they said that all mosques were to be blown up, what was the status of the mosque in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The mosque was blown up in a loud explosion which damaged many buildings around the mosque, shattering the glass, destroying windows and damaging the tiles on the roof-tops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's continue along this period, this spring and summer of 1992. Did you ever see any of the defendants in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you mean defendants or the wounded -- oh, defendants. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The accused. Did you see any of the accused in Bosanski Samac during that period in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I did see the people sitting here, the people I know, and assert that I know them, in the spring and summer of 1992. Mr. Zaric stayed in Samac until Odzak fell, in my books, or was liberated, in their books.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you saw Simo Zaric, how was he dressed? Was he in civilian clothes or uniform?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Mostly in uniform. I don't even remember seeing him in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about Miroslav Tadic? Did you ever see Miroslav Tadic in Bosanski Samac during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I used to see Miroslav Tadic from day one, from the day when Serbs entered into Samac and when they renamed it into Serbian Samac. From day one until the day when I crossed over into Croatia, I saw him all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you saw him, how was he dressed, in uniform or in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: In uniform. Long beard, mustache, the same mustache that he had had before, small glasses. He resembled Draza Mihajlovic. He wanted to resemble him on purpose. I would also like to add that in his right arm, he always had a Scorpion and his finger on the trigger, and that is how he was walking around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say he had a Scorpion, "He was carrying a Scorpion in his right hand, his finger on the trigger," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I asked some others and they explained to me that was a Scorpion. I saw it and I didn't know what it was. It looks like a rifle but it is very short, like this. It wasn't a rifle, but it wasn't a pistol either because it was a longer than a pistol. And he always had his index finger on the trigger, and that's how he was walking around at any time of day or night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during this period, you had just don't back a few days earlier before the war started, and over the next two, three months, how did you feel about this whole thing that was happening in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was very confused. I didn't know what was going on. At the first moment, I said it was the Croatian army, because I saw some soldiers in camouflage uniform, and that's why I assumed they were the Croatian army, and that is why I went to my neighbours, and I wanted to ask them, "What is the Croatian army doing here?" Since the war in Croatian was already going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was that the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't. I think it was the Yugoslav army, together with our local townspeople, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during those first three months, did something happen to the Croatian men in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Some time went by, very brief period, and then our phones were disconnected. Then they took all Croatian men and put them in the secondary school in Bosanski Samac. The Croatian women and children were taken to Crkvina, to the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did the Croatian women and children remain at the cultural centre in Crkvina? How long were they held there?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Maybe a day or two. They all returned home. The women and the children returned. The men did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said that they held Croatian men at the high school?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did you know Croatian men were being held at the high school?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: My neighbour, Ruzica, who worked at the job centre, and the people present here know them, the so-called Samac townspeople, she said that Pero was with -- that Pero told her that her husband had told Pero that he was at the high school, and he asked her to come to the high school and bring him some food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have any relatives that were being held at the high school?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. This Pero, my sister's in-law. The daughter of my sister is married to him. He's from Zasavica. He was there with two more brothers. All three brothers were detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me get this straight. Your sisters son-in-law and his two brothers were being held at the high school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in the beginning, were you able to visit these people at the high school, bring them any food?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Every day we would go and we brought them bedding, that is to say only the pillow and the covers so that they would have something to sleep on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you go with some of the others to bring food or bedding or whatever to the high school, to the prisoners at the high school?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I brought some things to Pero and his brothers the whole time they were there. The whole time they were detained, I would bring them things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you previously mentioned an older neighbour called Uncle Juro, the person you went to speak to on the first day. Approximately what age was he?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: He was very old, older than me. He's 10 or 15 years older than me. He was definitely over 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to him, Uncle Juro, this older man, during those first few days of the war?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. They took him along with the other Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was he held at the high school?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these people that were held, these Croatian prisoners, did you know these people from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I knew everybody who lived in Bosanski Samac. I didn't know all of the people from the villages. And there were both people from Bosanski Samac and the villages detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these Croatian prisoners that were being held at the high school, were these people soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: There were no Croats or Muslims amongst the soldiers except for the ones that were members of the 4th Detachment. Whether we were betrayed or liberated, whether they helped the ones that either liberated us or took us prisoner, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But these people who were being held, they were not soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Objection, Your Honours. Calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I don't think it's speculation. If she's known these people all her life, she can tell whether or not these people were soldiers or civilians

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a direct question from which the witness from her own knowledge can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: She's not an expert to make a difference between civilians and soldiers, Your Honour. That was my basis for the objection, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. The Trial Chamber will allow the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is, ma'am, these people, these Croatian prisoners that were -- these Croatians that were being held at the high school, were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They were civilians. Uncle Juro couldn't have been a soldier because he was more than 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If he was 15 -- approximately 15 years older than you, he would have to be about 75 years old at the time. Does that sound correct, his approximate age, about 75 years old?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was old. I don't know what year he was born, but he was very old. And the defendants know that as well. They know how old he was. He was at least over 60, maybe even over 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about the Croatian men that were being arrested and held. What about Muslim men? Were they being arrested?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: At that time, some Muslims were detained. We didn't know who was being detained. We had no information about that. But we found out that there were relatively few Muslims detained at the time while they were fighting with the Croats and trying to liquidate them and get -- rid them out of Bosnia. They weren't locking up Muslims at that particular time all that much. I don't know the schedule of when they were detaining whom, because we were never given any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly. When the Muslims were being detained -- let's start when Muslims were being detained, where were they being held in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Some Muslims were detained in the part of the primary school that didn't burn down. Some were detained at the TO, and some were detained at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have any relatives that were detained in any of those facilities, any of those prison camps?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Of course. Two sons of my oldest brother, my nephew who was -- who is a year older than me. His name is Alija Drljacic. He was also detained. And he was also in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just clarify this. Your -- is it your brother's name who is Alija Drljacic or you had a nephew named Alija Drljacic?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: My nephew's name is Alija Drljacic. My brother was called Safet and his two sons were called Hasan and Abdulah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they were all detained?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: With the others, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these three nephews, were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They were all civilians. How could they be soldiers? I don't know what they meant by Muslim extremists. I don't know what they meant to say when they said that we were all Muslim extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How were the Muslim men treated that were being held in these three prison camps, the TO, the SUP, and the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They know how they felt. But the neighbours heard their beatings, how they had to sing Chetnik songs, how they were screaming from the beatings. The neighbours could hear it, and then they would tell us everything. They would say, "Last night there was a lot of beating."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you received information from the neighbours or the people who live near the TO and the SUP or the people who live near the primary school? Who was providing this information as to the beatings that were going on?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: People that lived nearby, those who heard the beatings. They couldn't see anything, but they heard screams and the songs that they had to sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After you were exchanged, did you ever meet your nephew Avdo who had been held?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. He lived in Orasje. He is my nephew. My nephew Hasan I had not seen after that, but I know he's alive, and he lives somewhere in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where had your nephew Avdo been held, in which prison camps?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: First he was detained in the primary school. Then he was -- I don't know when he was transferred to the TO, but I know when he left the TO. I was an eyewitness to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did he go after the TO?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Their eyes were blindfolded, and they were taken on the bus, but I don't know what direction they went to. And later we found out they went to Batkovic, but they were all blindfolded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when did you see him after your release?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I saw him after I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know the month and year?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was exchanged on the 25th of December, 1993, and then after a few days I went directly to my daughters, and then after a few days I went to visit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did he appear?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Awful. And I had seen him after -- a year after he left. So he had a whole year to recuperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he look just like you recalled when you first -- when you saw him prior to the war? Did he look the same as when you saw him prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. They took out his teeth. He got very old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can have a break, Mr. Weiner. We've been sitting -- we can have a break up to 17.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just one thing, Your Honour. Could -- at about 6.00 or so could we see how the witness is feeling? Because of her age, I'm a little bit concerned about going long past 6.00. Just inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So you may be able to determine that during the break. So we will adjourn until 17.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Two matters, Your Honour. One is the translators handed me a note that a comment that was made in relation to -- I asked her what colour was Mr. Zaric's shirt and she answered what colour his hair was. And the translators have asked me to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes.
