utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It came with a sheet of paper. The other thing is once again, I would probably recommend around 6.00 maybe to break a little bit early because of her age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. She can't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you hear now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Weiner, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'd like to ask you a question. Earlier today when we started, I asked you a question concerning Simo Zaric's shirt, and I just spoke to the translators at the break, and you said his hair was grey. Let's just clarify that. What colour is Mr. Zaric's hair? Looking --

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: His hair is grey. I thought you were talking about his hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And his --

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: [In English] No. No listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what colour is his shirt?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His shirt is white.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify, Your Honour. That is the colour of hair and shirt of Mr. Zaric. So again she has properly identified the correct man, for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sometime no listen. Broken. [Interpretation] Yes. I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me right now?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you well now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. All right. Let us continue. From late April through the summer and fall of 1992, let's talk about the conditions as they existed in Bosanski Samac. Were Muslim men treated in a humiliating and -- in a humiliating manner?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Everybody, not only men but women too, had to work. They worked in places where they were degraded the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's discuss that. What do you mean that people were -- had to work -- men and women had to work in places in which they were degraded the most? Explain it, explain it to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Serbs called it the work obligation, but in fact it was forced labour. Forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's take some examples. Do you know a man by the name of Ahmet Hadzialijagic?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Hadzialijagic was the managing director of Jugobanka and the accused know this. He was made to perform manual, degrading jobs, such as street sweeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said he was the manager of a bank. Was that the Jugobanka?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Jugobanka, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said he had to do -- to perform degrading jobs such as sweeping. Where did he have to sweep in relation to Jugobanka where he had served as director?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Everywhere, including in the streets where Jugobanka was situated. Streets are very short and the distances are small. He had to work in the vicinity of his own bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Mirza Vejzovic? Mirza Vejzovic was one of the directors in the Samac textile industry. He was the sales director. He also did all sorts of degrading jobs, including the sweeping of the compound of the Samac textile industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So he had to sweep the compound of the same business that he had served as a director?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with a man from Bosanski Samac with the last name of Jusufovic?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Jusufovic used to be the director of the secondary school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that the same as a high school principal?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The -- the headmaster. He used to be a teacher, but he occupied the position of director or headmaster, principal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did they make him do?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: All times of manual work. And throughout the war, he had to load and unload from trucks, from warehouses into shops, anywhere. All sorts of humiliating jobs. That's what they called the work obligation, whereas in fact it was forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these three individuals that you just mentioned who were given menial tasks to perform, were these educated persons?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Exclusively. They were all educated persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All university trained?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: All university trained, those three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you see any Serbs during this same period being forced to sweep the streets?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Why, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You mentioned men that had to perform some forced labour. We were just talking about some men. What about women? Did Muslim or Croat women in Bosanski Samac have to perform forced labour?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I would only like to stress that Muslim men did all the hardest forms of labour, including the digging of trenches between the Serbs and the army of Bosnia -- army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And while you're talking about that, the digging of trenches between the two armies, was anyone ever injured while digging those trenches?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some people were wounded. Some were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's continue on with the women. Were women of Muslim and Croatian -- of the Muslim and Croatian ethnic group forced to work in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: All of them had received call-ups requiring them to report at a certain time. But let me emphasise that every Serb woman could easily order any Muslim woman to come to her place and clean her house and even wash her feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you know any Muslim women who had to go and do chores at the home of a civilian -- that were forced to do chores at the home of a civilian in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I knew all the women. I can't tell you specifically that this woman had to work at that time. But in any case, any Serb woman, man, or child had the power to order any Muslim anything. We had no right to object or complain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you of any -- were you aware of any cases, any of your friends who were just told by a Serb woman that they had to come to their house to clean, to wash, to iron, to perform any chores?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: She would address the people giving orders, and those people would then tell the women to do such-and-such a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "she would address," are you talking about a Serb woman who would go to the people who were assigning jobs and request labour?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. And a Serb woman could even say, "I want this woman in particular."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where would you go to make these requests for labourers?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, you were aware that -- however, were friends of yours, colleagues of yours forced to work in homes?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: All those people who worked had to sign those call-up papers indicating the time when they had to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this about the people who had to work: Do you know anyone who was paid for the work that they performed?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I don't know any such person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I don't think you're -- excuse me. I don't think your question has been directly answered as to whether the witness knows of any friends or relatives who were called upon to work in homes and so on. Perhaps if we could see whether there is a response to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Every woman, every woman who received the summons to report at a certain place at a certain time had to report and receive her orders as to what she would be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Here's the question. If you could just listen carefully. The question isn't whether or not you had to work, you had to report and work, is did you know people, did you know women as friends, relatives, neighbours, colleagues, that had to report and work in homes, in the homes of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: We all know -- every person in Samac knows everybody else. So everybody would tell the others, "I had been at such-and-such a place doing such-and-such a job."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you hear from anybody, did you yourself hear from anyone that they had to go to the home of a Serb and do certain work? Did you hear from anyone, either friends, relatives, colleagues, or neighbours?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I heard such things on several occasions. I can't recall anything specific now. But in any case, the accused are perfectly well aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Without referring to the accused, but you had heard, people had told you, although you can't recall anything specific now, people had told you back then about this, about being forced to work in someone else's home?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Women worked in other people's homes on the orders of the housewife in question, the owner of that home who needed somebody to do the housecleaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you knew some of these women?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I have already told you that we all know each other in Samac. Samac is a small place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you give us any names of such women who worked in the homes of Serb women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you the name of this or that woman in specific, but that was the practice at the time, and we would all tell each other who had been doing what and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue on. Maybe we'll look at this topic again tomorrow, but let's continue on for a little while. Teufik Drljacic, is that --

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Teufik Drljacic is my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he living in Bosanski Samac in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: My brother has lived -- lived in Bosanski Samac since the day he was born until he left Samac in the course of an exchange on the 24th, and on the 25th, we crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So he was exchanged with you in December 24th or December 25th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's correct. We were the last from my family to be exchanged. And it wasn't an exchange. It was expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that a little bit later. But let's talk about your brother. What did he do for work?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Before the war, my brother owned his own glazing business. And after the so-called liberation by the Serbs, all the businesses were looted, and his shop was taken over. He, however, had to do all kinds of jobs in his line of work, both in town and outside town, using his own material without getting paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take it one step at a time. Your brother had a shop. Was that shop located in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The shop was in Bosanski Samac, in Vuk Karadzic Street. I don't remember the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that was a glazier shop where they fix glass and mirrors?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what happened after the war started in April of 1992? Was his shop closed or did someone take it over?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: He got a new boss by the name of Milos. Milos was a man from Tisina, and he became the manager, whereas my brother became his worker, his employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, prior to Milos being made your brother's new boss, wasn't your brother his own boss? Wasn't that your brother's shop?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. The shop belonged to him, but that other man became his boss and gave him orders. My brother had to do whatever Milos wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who appointed -- who took your brother's business away and appointed Milos as his boss?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This Milos who was appointed your brother's boss of your brother's own business, where was he from? Was he from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: He was from Tisina, the village nearest to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when was your brother's shop confiscated?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The same day. The day when we were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, was your brother forced to work at the shop and at other locations?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Certainly. He didn't work only in Samac. He worked in Obudovac, in Odzak as well, when Mr. Zaric was some sort of commander in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did he do in Odzak when the defendant Simo Zaric was a commander there?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: He worked as a glass cutter, as a glazier. He repaired windows. He made windowpanes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did he work during the day, or day and night, or when did he work?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, if he went to Odzak, he would spend the day there. But at any time of day and night whenever some Serb's windows were damaged by shelling, he would be summoned to go there and do the repair. He didn't dare ask where he was going and when he would be back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he work on the weekends?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: At any time. I've already told you. At any time of day or night. And everybody had to work weekends too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was your brother ever paid for the work that he performed in Bosanski Samac, Obudovac, or in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Nobody was paid. So he couldn't have been paid either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about for the materials that had been in his shop after his shop was confiscated? Was he ever paid for those materials?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about for his shop? Was your brother ever paid for his shop after it was confiscated?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Never. His wife, his ex-wife, rather, was the owner of the shop. Whether she got it back, I don't know. I think she did, actually. But it is still occupied by some displaced Serbs, refugees who were driven out of somewhere. I don't know exactly. Because it's a building with a yard, which was a residential building before it was turned into a business. And when it stopped working for lack of materials, it -- some Serbs moved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like to break here or do you want me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If the witness is okay -- is feeling well to continue, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How are you feeling, Mrs. Drljacic? Are you feeling all right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Well, since -- since I'm here, I can't feel well, but I think I'll make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps we can proceed another half hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you said you think that his ex-wife got it back, are you talking about recently or are you talking about back around 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about a recent period. Maybe about a year ago. Maybe. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. One last question about that. After your brother's shop was confiscated, was your brother paid any rent by this Milos from Tisina for using your brother's shop?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: He didn't use it for his own needs. He did it by his boss's orders. He was also told where he would work. This shop was not called the shop of Milos.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. Did Milos ever pay your brother rent?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: No, he never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. From late April of 1992 through the end of the year and even into 1993, were houses in Bosanski Samac vacant? Were apartments or houses vacant?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: So this is how it goes: Men that were of a military age were immediately called to get arms to defend the Serbian country. However, those who already knew what this was all about wanted to resist, and they tried to leave by swimming across the River Sava. Those who did not respond to the draft call and who didn't take up arms had to go to work. In that case, the family of those that left, that swam across the Sava River, were rounded up, taken to a camp in the village of Zasavica. Women, older men, and children were allegedly there, although there were men also amongst the older people. They were over 60, 70, and maybe 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to get this clear. One of the reasons for vacancies is that where men had swum across the Sava River, their families were then removed from their homes and brought to Zasavica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what happened. Then these empty houses would be immediately looted. And the accused are well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Before we get on to the looting let's just continue on with the vacancies. But tell us, what was Zasavica? You mentioned Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Zasavica is a Croatian village. It was completely vacated. Maybe only five or six Croats were left in the village. And this entire village was turned into something that they called an isolation area. Actually, this was a camp in -- where women, children, and as I said, some older people were detain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said "they called it an isolation area." Who was calling it an isolation area?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said it was a camp. Why would you call it a camp?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: What else could it be? It was a camp. People were detained there, and they weren't allowed to leave unless they wanted to be exchanged. And if they were exchanged, then they would have to leave their homes and all their property behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue on with the vacancies. Were vacancies caused as a result of arrests?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Certainly. A house that was vacant or if the families were already moved to the camps, those houses were looted. If some of the Serbs left their houses or their apartments and moved into a bigger apartment or a better house, then they would behave as if they were in their own property. They would take the furniture and everything else out of the homes. When their refugees started arriving from other areas, they would even put these refugees up in the empty houses that were also ruined sometimes because windows and doors would be stripped off and only bare calls would remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to the looting in a little while. I just want to first find out why these homes were vacant before the looting occurred. Now, were Muslims or Croats evicted in Bosanski Samac, which resulted in homes becoming vacant? Were Muslims or Croats evicted in 1992 or 1993, resulting in homes becoming vacant?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone who was ever evicted?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I don't know that there are some people that weren't evicted. Those that weren't evicted are very few and far between.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you evicted from your apartment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was evicted three months -- three and a half months before I left Samac. I was evicted into the street practically. I didn't know that the Red Cross had found out about Zasavica, so they couldn't put any more people there, which is why they couldn't take me to Zasavica, and I had to live on the street. I was very sick. These two men here that I recognised can confirm how I looked, how I felt and what I looked like when I was evicted from my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, can we find out whether this was the International Committee of the Red Cross or the national Red Cross of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that the Red Cross -- ma'am, you said that the Red Cross had found out about Zasavica and as a result, they couldn't put any more people there. Which Red Cross are you referring to, the International Red Cross or the local Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The International Red Cross from Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about your eviction. Could you tell the Court the circumstances of your eviction, how it came about? Please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I was at my brother's Teufik. He had to go to work, and I was cooking for him and myself. He had a stove, and he had wood, firewood, so we could cook at his place. Since we will no electricity and water, I would go to his apartment and cook for him there. I also cooked for him because he was left alone. And he couldn't be exchanged because he had this work obligation. His wife and his daughter could leave. They were not under a work obligation. So I was at my brother's. Then two soldiers came. They were very young. I felt really bad for them. They were armed, and they asked me what my name was. I gave them my name, and they said that I should return to my apartment. At that moment, my brother came in for breakfast, and I said that I didn't want to go until Piko, that's what we called him, until Piko came to have lunch. My brother immediately realised that I had to go, and he gave me a sign with his eyes that I should go, but I kept saying I don't want to go until you come home for lunch. But then eventually I did go with them. I can show you what state I was in when I was going towards my house flanked by two armed soldiers. Actually, they weren't soldiers, they were policemen. Can I show you what condition I was in when I was going towards my apartment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think what she wants to demonstrate is at one point she could barely walk. She was bent over. And she had demonstrated it for me. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure, you can demonstrate for the Court your condition at that time. You can demonstrate for the Court your condition at that time, how you were walking.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: I had to use a cane in one hand, but that wasn't enough support. And because of my great pain, I was holding my other knee, and this is how I went home flanked by two armed policemen, came to my apartment. I apologise. Could you hear what I said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone could hear what you said. Okay. So the two policemen escort you to your apartment. Was it a long distance from your brother's apartment to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: The distance was about 150 to 200 metres, maybe a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you got home with these two officers. What did you do when you reached your building? What happened?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: We came to my apartment. I opened the door. They asked for the key. I gave it to them. And that's when they relieved me of my apartment. I had no right to get it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what did they say? You said they relieved you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you go on, Mr. Weiner, can we agree on the demonstration of how the witness was walking?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, the witness was standing with her back bent over. She was went over, and she seemed to be -- she indicated that she had, I think, her left hand holding her knee with her right hand was holding a stick or a cane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And that's how she walked all the way to her apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for not clarifying the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you walked to your apartment. You got there, and they told you -- they took the keys from you. What did they say? Why -- why couldn't you have your apartment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: That's correct. They didn't have to say anything to me. This was normal procedure. These two soldiers, they were two young kids. And I asked them about the following: I told them, "See what I have in this apartment. Apart from my regular job, I earned a lot of money also from my -- from being a seamstress. Would you please let me take my sewing machine with me?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they let you take your sewing machine?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They did, but I said that I couldn't carry it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did someone come and pick up your sewing machine?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC
utterances.text: They asked me, "What do you want? Do you want us to carry it for you?" I said, "Well, maybe my brother." And they said, "Well, where is your brother?" And I said, "Well, he is doing his work obligation. Maybe when he's done he could come." They said, "Well, can he come around 7.00?" I said, "Well, if he's back at 7.00, he will come." And that's indeed what happened. My brother came with a little wheelbarrow, trailer, and he loaded this sewing machine on it. He was met by some man while he was walking from his house to my apartment, and this man asked him, "What is your name?" Because he thought it was a little bit suspicious that he had a sewing machine. And my brother said, "Teufik Drljacic." And then this man beat him severely. And then when this man saw that another man called Vajzovic Sead was watching him beating my brother, then this man said, "You monkey, why are you looking at me? Get away from the window."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can adjourn at this time. We will adjourn and continue the proceedings tomorrow at 14.15 hours. The Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
